summary: Defines a Mobile IPv4 mechanism for a mobility agent to tell another agent serving the same mobile node that the registration has ended. A home agent can also use it to end a registration. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: If you move to a new house, your old post office should be told to stop forwarding your mail. This memo lets the agents in Mobile IP tell each other when a registration is cancelled.

subtitle: How Mobile IPv4 agents tell each other, with acknowledgment, that a mobile node's registration has been cut short.

tldr.problem: In Mobile IPv4, a home agent or foreign agent may stop serving a mobile node, but the other agent only finds out when the binding expires, which wastes resources and skews accounting.
tldr.mechanism: Agents advertise support with an 'X' bit, negotiate it with a Revocation Support Extension, and then send an authenticated, replay-protected Registration Revocation message (type 7) that the receiver answers with an acknowledgment (type 15).
tldr.outcome: Resources can be released promptly and the mobile node can be told sooner that service has ended. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and introduces no new error codes.

facts.label: Rate limit
facts.value: One message per second per binding

today: RFC 3543 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It builds on RFC 3344, the Mobile IPv4 specification.

sections.title: Why Revoke a Registration
sections.content:
Mobile IP registers a mobile node's location so it can keep communicating with its home domain. At any time the home agent or the foreign agent may wish to stop servicing the mobile node, or may no longer be required to. This RFC defines a general registration revocation mechanism by which one mobility agent notifies another (or a 'direct' co-located mobile node) that a binding is terminated.

The RFC lists four advantages:

  • Timely release of Mobile IP resources, instead of waiting for the binding to expire.
  • Accurate accounting, because the actual end of the registration is relayed.
  • Earlier adoption of domain policy changes, such as a home domain that now requires reverse tunnels.
  • Quicker notice to the mobile node, shortening any 'black-hole' period.

Since many mobile nodes may not understand revocation, care was taken to keep backwards compatibility with RFC 3344.
sections.eli5: Without a way to say 'stop', the old helper keeps working for someone who has already left until the clock runs out. Telling it right away saves effort and keeps the records honest.

sections.title: Revocation Versus Deregistration
sections.content:
The RFC defines revocation as the premature termination of a mobility binding. A mobility agent is the home agent or foreign agent of RFC 3344. A 'direct' co-located mobile node registers directly with its home agent with the 'D' bit set, not through a foreign agent.

Revocation does not replace deregistration. Deregistration is how a mobile node tells its home agent that, for example, it has roamed back to its home subnet. Revocation is a signal between mobility agents. A mobile node that wants to end its own binding MUST NOT send a revocation message and should deregister as RFC 3344 describes. A direct co-located mobile node may process revocation messages it receives, since they are useful to trigger renegotiation of required services, but it MUST NOT send one.
sections.eli5: Leaving by yourself and saying goodbye is one thing. Someone else telling the helpers 'this person is no longer yours to serve' is another. This memo is only about the second.

sections.title: Advertising and Negotiating Support
sections.content:
A mobility agent shows it supports revocation by setting a new X bit in its Agent Advertisement. A foreign agent that sets it MUST support the Revocation Support Extension, revocation messages and revocation acknowledgments on that link.

Support is then negotiated per registration with the Revocation Support Extension (type 137), carrying a Timestamp and an I bit. A foreign agent that advertises X and has a security association with the home agent MUST attach it to the forwarded registration request. A home agent that wants revocation MUST attach it to the registration reply. Revocation is negotiated for a binding when both sides have included the extension in a successful registration exchange. A mobile node that is not co-located MUST NOT include one.

The I bit is optional. When both agents set it, the home agent may decide whether the mobile node is informed of a revocation. The extension is skippable, and it MUST be protected by an authentication extension or an equivalent such as AAA or IPsec.
sections.eli5: Before anyone can cancel anything, both helpers have to agree they speak this language. Each one hangs up a sign, and they swap notes during sign-up to confirm.

sections.title: Revocation and Acknowledgment Messages
sections.content:
Both messages are Mobile IP control messages sent over UDP to destination port 434. A Registration Revocation message is type 7 and carries an A bit (0 if the revoking agent is the foreign agent, 1 if it is the home agent), an I bit, the Home Address, the Home Domain Address, the Foreign Domain Address and a 32-bit Revocation Identifier, followed by extensions and an authenticator.

The Registration Revocation Acknowledgment is type 15. It copies the Home Address and Revocation Identifier from the message it answers so the revoker can match them, and its I bit may be 1 only if it was 1 in the revocation. A valid, authenticated revocation MUST be answered with an acknowledgment.

Both messages MUST carry a valid authenticator (a home-foreign authenticator between agents, or a mobile-home authenticator to a direct co-located mobile node) or another equally secure mechanism such as IPsec. Anything not adequately protected MUST be silently discarded. A revocation MUST NOT be sent for an expired registration, and an agent MUST NOT send more than one revocation or registration message per second for the same binding.
sections.eli5: The cancel note says who is cancelling, whose mail it is, and where it was being sent, plus a time stamp. The reply copies back the name and the stamp so the sender knows which note was received.

sections.title: Who Does What
sections.content:
When the home agent revokes, it sets A to 1 and sends the message to the foreign domain address. If it wants the foreign agent to tell the mobile node it sets I to 1, and if not, to 0. The foreign agent checks the authenticator, the A bit and the identifier, locates the binding and the registration timestamp that must precede the revocation, revokes it, frees its resources and sends an acknowledgment.

When the foreign agent revokes, it sets A to 0. If the I bit was negotiated, it sets I to 1 to ask the home agent whether the mobile node should be informed. The home agent validates the message, frees resources, and acknowledges, setting I to 1 if it wants the mobile node informed.

A direct co-located mobile node validates the message, SHOULD first send the acknowledgment, and may then stop any reverse tunnel and release its resources.

If no acknowledgment arrives in a reasonable time the revoker MUST retransmit. Each retransmission updates the timestamp in the identifier and any authenticator derived from it, is sent at most once per second per binding, SHOULD use exponential backoff, and MUST NOT continue beyond the normal life of the binding.
sections.eli5: Whoever cancels sends the note, and the other side checks it is real, shuts down the service and writes back. If there is no reply, the sender keeps trying, a bit slower each time, until the booking would have ended anyway.

sections.title: Telling the Mobile Node
sections.content:
A foreign agent can use a mechanism that already exists in RFC 3344: the sequence number in agent advertisements. A restarted agent begins again at 0, so a mobile node presumes it lost its bindings and re-registers. A foreign agent can deliberately send a unicast agent advertisement with sequence number 0 to a mobile node to signal that its binding no longer exists, and MAY also set the B (busy) bit to 1 so the node tries another agent.

Two registration bits need care. A foreign agent that wants to revoke registrations MUST set the R bit in its advertisements, but SHOULD deny a co-located mobile node that registers through it as 'Administratively Prohibited'. Revocation is not supported for a co-located node with the D bit set that registers via a foreign agent, because the home agent cannot be sure the source address really is the serving foreign agent, which could allow a man-in-the-middle denial-of-service attack.
sections.eli5: The foreign agent can quietly tell a visitor 'I forgot you' by acting as if it had just restarted. The visitor then looks for another helper.

sections.title: Replay Protection and Security
sections.content:
Revocation ends service, so replay protection is crucial. The RFC names two attacks by a man-in-the-middle: malicious repeaters, who replay a captured message later, and malicious reflectors, who send a message back to its originator. All revocations and acknowledgments MUST be both authenticated and replay-protected.

The defense is the 32-bit Revocation Identifier, a timestamp from the same clock used in the agent's revocation extensions, together with the A bit. The receiver checks that a message is not a replay or a reflection of one it sent, and silently discards replays. Because it is a timestamp, an agent can judge it without remembering all earlier identifiers. Identifiers from different agents need not be unique, and a match MUST NOT cause a revocation to be ignored. Datagrams may arrive out of order, so a suitable time window should be defined if increasing values are used.

The RFC also notes that agent advertisements can be spoofed on the link, tricking mobile nodes into thinking they were revoked. It advises discarding advertisements whose TTL is not 1 or that do not come from the same link address as other advertisements from that agent. It concludes that revocation is at least as secure as home-foreign authenticated registration, adding no new threats beyond compromise of the shared secret.
sections.eli5: A cancel note must be signed and dated. The date stops a villain from saving an old note and showing it again later, or bouncing your own note back at you.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
The RFC reserves two Mobile IP message types and one extension. Registration Revocation is type 7 and Registration Revocation Acknowledgment is type 15, both on UDP port 434, taken from the same number space as Registration Request (1) and Registration Reply (3).

The Revocation Support Extension is value 137, which MUST be in the skippable range (128 to 255) defined in RFC 3344. No new error codes are introduced, because a revocation is a notice that service has ended, not a request to stop it.
sections.eli5: Each new kind of message gets its own numbered slot in a shared list so nobody mixes them up. No new error messages were needed.
